Method of Attack: Phishing attacks using Microsoft Sway service to trick victims into giving Office 365 login credentials
Use of phishing kit offered as malware-as-a-service (MaaS)
Sending emails with benign PDF attachments impersonating Office 365 notifications
Redirecting victims from Sway presentations to phishing pages mimicking Microsoft Single Sign-on
Harvesting credentials and delivering them to separate data servers with real-time notification
Follow-up operations including logging into compromised accounts, dumping email data, and sending forged PDFs to victim's contacts
Impacted Systems: Small and medium financial services companies
Attack Vector: Phishing emails from compromised external business partner accounts with benign PDF attachments
Use of Microsoft Sway service to host realistic-looking documents
Redirects to phishing sites disguised as Microsoft Single Sign-on pages
Indicators of Compromise: Emails of at least 27 adversaries found in phishing kit variants
Phishing kit frontend uses old Microsoft Outlook login page version 6.7.6640.0 from 2017
Emails with sender and recipient as same person with true recipients hidden in BCC
Phishing pages hosted on Microsoft Sway
Separate data server receiving harvested credentials with notification email addresses in code
